{{Short description|Massive fermion wave equation in Kerr spacetime}}
'''Chandrasekhar–Page equations''' describe the wave function of the [[spin-1/2]] [[massive particle]]s, that resulted by seeking a separable solution to the [[Dirac equation]] in [[Kerr metric]] or [[Kerr–Newman metric]]. In 1976, [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] showed that a separable solution can be obtained from the [[Dirac equation]] in [[Kerr metric]].<ref>{{cite journal | title=The solution of Dirac's equation in Kerr geometry | journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences | publisher=The Royal Society | volume=349 | issue=1659 | date=1976-06-29 | issn=2053-9169 | doi=10.1098/rspa.1976.0090 | pages=571–575| bibcode=1976RSPSA.349..571C | last1=Chandrasekhar | first1=S. | s2cid=122791570 }}</ref> Later, [[Don Page (physicist)|Don Page]] extended this work to [[Kerr–Newman metric]], that is applicable to charged black holes.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Page | first=Don N. | title=Dirac equation around a charged, rotating black hole | journal=Physical Review D | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=14 | issue=6 | date=1976-09-15 | issn=0556-2821 | doi=10.1103/physrevd.14.1509 | pages=1509–1510| bibcode=1976PhRvD..14.1509P }}</ref> In his paper, Page notices that N. Toop also derived his results independently, as informed to him by Chandrasekhar. Incidentally, while solving this problem, Chandrasekhar discovered a separable solution to the [[Dirac equation]] in flat space-time in [[oblate spheroidal coordinates]] for the first time.

By assuming a [[normal mode]] decomposition of the form <math>e^{i(m\phi-\omega t)}</math> (with <math>m</math> being the azimuthal component of the particle angular momentum and takes half integer values and with <math>\omega</math> being the frequency) for the time and the azimuthal component of the spherical polar coordinates <math>(r,\theta,\phi)</math>, Chandrasekhar showed that the four [[Dirac spinor]] components of the wave function,

:<math> \begin{bmatrix} F_1(r,\theta) \\ F_2(r,\theta) \\ G_1(r,\theta) \\ G_2(r,\theta)\end{bmatrix}e^{i(m\phi-\omega t)}</math>

can be expressed as product of radial and angular functions. The [[separation of variables]] is effected for the functions <math>f_1=(r-ia\cos\theta)F_1</math>, <math>f_2=(r-ia\cos\theta)F_2</math>, <math>g_1=(r+ia\cos\theta)G_1</math> and <math>g_2=(r+ia\cos\theta)G_2</math> (with <math>a</math> being the [[angular momentum]] per unit mass of the black hole) as in 

:<math>f_1(r,\theta) = R_{-}(r)S_{-}(\theta), \quad f_2(r,\theta) = R_{+}(r)S_{+}(\theta),</math>
:<math>g_1(r,\theta) = R_{+}(r)S_{-}(\theta), \quad g_2(r,\theta) = R_{-}(r)S_{+}(\theta).</math>

== Chandrasekhar–Page angular equations ==

The angular functions satisfy the coupled eigenvalue equations,<ref name="chandra">Chandrasekhar, S.,(1983). The mathematical theory of black holes. Clarenden Press, Section 104</ref>

:<math>
\begin{align}
\mathcal{L}_{\frac{1}{2}} S_{+} &= -(\lambda - a\mu \cos\theta )S_{-}, \\
\mathcal{L}_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\dagger} S_{-} &= +(\lambda + a\mu \cos\theta )S_{+},
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>\mu</math> is the particle's [[rest mass]] (measured in units so that it is the inverse of the [[Compton wavelength]]), and

:<math>\mathcal{L}_n = \frac{{d}}{{d}\theta} + ( m \csc\theta - a\omega\sin\theta)  + n\cot \theta,  </math>
:<math>\mathcal{L}_n^{\dagger} = \frac{{d}}{{d}\theta} - (m \csc\theta- a\omega\sin\theta)  + n\cot\theta.</math>

Eliminating <math>S_{+}(\theta)</math> between the two equations, one obtains

:<math>\left(\mathcal{L}_{\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{L}_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\dagger} + \frac{a\mu\sin\theta}{\lambda + a\mu\cos\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\dagger} + \lambda^2 - a^2\mu^2\cos^2\theta\right) S_{-} = 0.</math>

The function <math>S_{+}</math> satisfies the [[adjoint equation]], that can be obtained from the above equation by replacing <math>\theta</math> with <math>\pi-\theta</math>. The boundary conditions for these second-order differential equations are that <math>S_{-}</math>(and <math>S_{+}</math>) be regular at <math>\theta=0</math> and <math>\theta=\pi</math>. The eigenvalue problem presented here in general requires numerical integrations for it to be solved. 

===Properties and limiting solutions===

The eigenvalue problem depends on two continuous parameters, namely <math>a\omega</math> and <math>a\mu</math>. For a given <math>a\omega</math> and <math>a\mu</math>, the eigenstates are characterised by three discrete numbers: the particle angular momentum, <math>j=1/2,3/2,\dots</math>, its azimuthal component <math>m=-j,-j+1,\dots,j-1,j</math> and the parity <math>\mathcal{P}=\pm 1.</math> The spectrum elements may then be explicitly labelled as<ref>Dolan, S. R., & Gair, J. R. (2009). The massive Dirac field on a rotating black hole spacetime: angular solutions. Classical and Quantum Gravity, 26(17), 175020.</ref>

:<math>S_\pm = {}_{s=\pm\frac{1}{2}} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\mu)}, \lambda = \lambda_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\mu)}.</math>

The eigenvalue <math>\lambda</math> has the physical interpretation of being the [[square root]] of the generalised total anagular momentum squared.<ref>Batic, D., & Schmid, H. (2005). Chandrasekhar separation ansatz and the generalized total angular momentum for the Dirac equation in the Kerr-Newman metric. arXiv preprint gr-qc/0512112.</ref> The knowledge of the spectrum in the positive quadrant <math>a\omega>0,a\mu>0</math> is sufficient to determine the full spectrum, as implied by the symmetry:

:<math>\lambda_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\mu)}=-\lambda_{j,-m,-\mathcal{P}}^{(-a\omega,a\mu)}=-\lambda_{j,m,-\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,-a\mu)}=\lambda_{j,-m,\mathcal{P}}^{(-a\omega,-a\mu)}.</math>

Furthermore

:<math>{}_{s} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\mu)}(\theta) = (-1)^{s-1/2}{}_{s} S_{j,m,-\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,-a\mu)}(\Theta)=\mathcal{P}(-1)^{m-1/2}{}_{-s} S_{j,-m,-\mathcal{P}}^{(-a\omega,a\mu)}(\theta)=\mathcal{P}(-1)^{j+m}{}_{-s} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\mu)}(\pi-\theta)</math>

and the combinations thereof.

'''Non-rotating black hole ([[Schwarzschild black hole]]) <math>a=0</math>''': The problem can be solved explicitly. The eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are given by

:<math>\lambda_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}=\mathcal{P}(j+1/2),</math>
:<math>\begin{bmatrix} {}_{+1/2} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}(\theta)\\ {}_{-1/2} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}(\theta)\end{bmatrix} = A\begin{bmatrix}\cos\frac{\theta}{2} & \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\-\sin\frac{\theta}{2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P_{j+\mathcal{P}/2}^{m+1/2}(\cos\theta) \\ c_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}P_{j+\mathcal{P}/2}^{m-1/2}(\cos\theta)\end{bmatrix},</math>

where <math>P</math> is the [[associated Legendre polynomials]] and

:<math>c_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}=\mathcal{P}(j+\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)-m, \quad A = \sqrt{\frac{(j-m)!}{2\pi(j+m)!}}.</math>

'''Special case <math>\omega=\pm \mu</math>''': For the special case where <math>\omega=+ \mu</math>, the solutions are given by<ref>{{cite journal |last=Chakrabarti|first= S. K.| title=On mass-dependent spheroidal harmonics of spin one-half | journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences | publisher=The Royal Society | volume=391 | issue=1800 | date=1984-01-09 | issn=2053-9169 | doi=10.1098/rspa.1984.0002 | pages=27–38|jstor=2397528|bibcode= 1984RSPSA.391...27C|s2cid= 120673756}}</ref>

:<math>\lambda_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\omega)}=-\frac{1}{2}+\mathcal{P}\sqrt{(j+\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)^2-2ma\omega+a^2\omega^2},</math>
:<math>\begin{bmatrix} {}_{+1/2} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}(\theta)\\ {}_{-1/2} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}(\theta)\end{bmatrix} = A\begin{bmatrix}\cos\frac{\theta}{2} & \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\-\sin\frac{\theta}{2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P_{j+\mathcal{P}/2}^{m+1/2}(\cos\theta) \\ c_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\omega)}P_{j+\mathcal{P}/2}^{m-1/2}(\cos\theta)\end{bmatrix},</math>

where

:<math>c_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\omega)}=[(j+\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)^2-m^2]/(\lambda_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,a\omega)}+m+1/2-a\omega), </math>
:<math> A = \sqrt{\frac{(j+\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)}{2\pi}\frac{(j+\mathcal{P}/2-m-1/2)!}{(j+\mathcal{P}/2+m+1/2)!}\left(1+\frac{\mathcal{P}(m-a\omega)}{\sqrt{(j+\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)^2-2ma\omega+a^2\omega^2}}\right)}\,.</math>

When <math>\omega=-\mu</math>, we have

:<math>\lambda_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,-a\omega)}=\frac{1}{2}+\mathcal{P}\sqrt{(j+\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)^2-2ma\omega+a^2\omega^2},</math>
:<math>\begin{bmatrix} {}_{+1/2} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,-a\omega)}(\theta)\\ {}_{-1/2} S_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(0,0)}(\theta)\end{bmatrix} = A\begin{bmatrix}\cos\frac{\theta}{2} & -\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\\sin\frac{\theta}{2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}P_{j+\mathcal{P}/2}^{m+1/2}(\cos\theta) \\ c_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,-a\omega)}P_{j+\mathcal{P}/2}^{m-1/2}(\cos\theta)\end{bmatrix},</math>

where

:<math>c_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,-a\omega)}=-[(j-\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)^2-m^2]/(-\lambda_{j,m,\mathcal{P}}^{(a\omega,-a\omega)}+m+1/2-a\omega), </math>
:<math> A = \sqrt{\frac{(j-\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)}{2\pi}\frac{(j-\mathcal{P}/2-m-1/2)!}{(j-\mathcal{P}/2+m+1/2)!}\left(1-\frac{\mathcal{P}(m-a\omega)}{\sqrt{(j-\mathcal{P}/2+1/2)^2-2ma\omega+a^2\omega^2}}\right)}\,.</math>

== Chandrasekhar–Page radial equations ==

For convenience, let us write <math>\sigma=-\omega.</math> The radial equations are given by{{r|chandra}}

:<math>
\begin{align}
\Delta^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{D}_{0} R_{-\frac{1}{2}} &= (\lambda +i\mu r)\Delta^{\frac{1}{2}}R_{+\frac{1}{2}}, \\
\Delta^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{D}_{0}^\dagger R_{+\frac{1}{2}} &= (\lambda -i\mu r)R_{-\frac{1}{2}},
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>\Delta = r^2 - 2Mr + a^2,</math> <math>M</math> is the black hole mass,

:<math>\mathcal{D}_n = \frac{{d}}{{d}r} + \frac{iK}{\Delta} + 2n \frac{r-M}{\Delta}, \quad \mathcal{D}_n^\dagger = \frac{{d}}{{d}r} - \frac{iK}{\Delta} + 2n \frac{r-M}{\Delta},</math>

and <math>K = (r^2+a^2)\sigma + am.</math> Eliminating <math>\Delta^{\frac{1}{2}}  R_{+\frac{1}{2}}</math> from the two equations, we obtain

:<math>\left(\Delta\mathcal{D}_{\frac{1}{2}}^\dagger\mathcal{D}_{0} - \frac{i\mu \Delta}{\lambda + i\mu r}\mathcal{D}_0 -\lambda^2 - \mu^2r^2\right) R_{-\frac{1}{2}} = 0.</math>

The function <math>\Delta^{\frac{1}{2}}  R_{+\frac{1}{2}}</math> satisfies the corresponding complex-conjugate equation.

===Reduction to one-dimensional scattering problem===
The problem of solving the radial functions for a particular eigenvalue of <math>\lambda</math> of the angular functions can be reduced to a problem of reflection and transmission as in one-dimensional [[Schrödinger equation]]; see also [[Regge–Wheeler–Zerilli equations]]. Particularly, we end up with the equations

:<math>\left(\frac{d^2}{d\hat r_*^2} + \sigma^2\right) Z^{\pm} = V^{\pm} Z^{\pm},</math>

where the Chandrasekhar–Page potentials <math>V^\pm</math> are defined by{{r|chandra}}

:<math>V^{\pm} = W^2 \pm \frac{dW}{d\hat r_*}, \quad W = \frac{\Delta^{\frac{1}{2}}(\lambda + \mu^2r^2)^{3/2}}{\varpi^2(\lambda^2+\mu^2r^2) + \lambda\mu\Delta/2\sigma},</math>

and <math>\hat r_*=r_*+\tan^{-1}(\mu r/\lambda)/2\sigma</math>, <math>r_*=r+2M\ln(r/2M-1)</math> is the [[Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates#Tortoise coordinate|tortoise coordinate]] and  <math>\varpi^2 = r^2+a^2 + am/\sigma</math>. The functions <math>Z^{\pm}(\hat r_*)</math> are defined by <math>Z^\pm = \psi^+ \pm \psi^-</math>, where

:<math>\psi^+ = \Delta^{\frac{1}{2}} R_{+\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{exp}\left(+\frac{i}{2}\tan^{-1} \frac{\mu r}{\lambda}\right), \quad \psi^- =  R_{-\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{i}{2}\tan^{-1} \frac{\mu r}{\lambda}\right).</math>

Unlike the [[Regge–Wheeler–Zerilli equations|Regge–Wheeler–Zerilli potentials]], the Chandrasekhar–Page potentials do not vanish for <math>r\to\infty</math>, but has the behaviour

:<math>V^\pm = \mu^2\left(1 - \frac{2M}{r} + \cdots\right).</math>

As a result, the corresponding asymptotic behaviours for <math>Z^\pm</math> as <math>r\to\infty</math> becomes

:<math>Z^\pm = \mathrm{exp}\left\{\pm i \left[(\sigma^2-\mu^2)^{1/2}r+ \frac{M\mu^2}{(\sigma^2-\mu^2)^{1/2}}\ln \frac{r}{2M}\right]\right\}.</math>
